In [[graph theory]], a '''fractional matching''' is a generalization of a [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]] in which, intuitively, each vertex may be broken into fractions that are matched to different neighbor vertices.

== Definition ==
Given a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] <math>G=(V,E)</math>, a fractional matching in <math>G</math> is a function that assigns, to each edge <math>e\in E</math>, a fraction <math>f(e)\in[0,1]</math>, such that for every vertex <math>v\in V</math>, the sum of fractions of edges adjacent to <math>v</math> is at most one:<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Aharoni|first1=Ron|last2=Kessler|first2=Ofra|date=1990-10-15|title=On a possible extension of Hall's theorem to bipartite hypergraphs|journal=Discrete Mathematics|language=en|volume=84|issue=3|pages=309–313|doi=10.1016/0012-365X(90)90136-6|issn=0012-365X|doi-access=free}}</ref> 
<math display="block">\forall v\in V: \sum_{e\ni v}f(e)\leq 1</math> 
A matching in the traditional sense is a special case of a fractional matching, in which the fraction of every edge is either zero or one: <math>f(e)=1</math> if <math>e</math> is in the matching, and <math>f(e)=0</math> if it is not.  For this reason, in the context of fractional matchings, usual matchings are sometimes called ''integral matchings''.

==Size==
The size of an integral matching is the number of edges in the matching, and the matching number <math>\nu(G)</math> of a graph <math>G</math> is the largest size of a matching in <math>G</math>.  Analogously, the ''size'' of a fractional matching is the sum of fractions of all edges.  The '''fractional matching number''' of a graph <math>G</math> is the largest size of a fractional matching in <math>G</math>. It is often denoted by <math>\nu^*(G)</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Liu|first1=Yan|last2=Liu|first2=Guizhen|date=2002|title=The fractional matching numbers of graphs|journal=Networks|language=en|volume=40|issue=4|pages=228–231|doi=10.1002/net.10047|s2cid=43698695 |issn=1097-0037}}</ref> Since a matching is a special case of a fractional matching, the integral matching number of every graph <math>G</math> is less than or equal to the fractional matching number of <math>G</math>; in symbols:<math display = block>\nu(G) \leq \nu^*(G).</math>A graph in which <math>\nu(G) = \nu^*(G)</math> is called a ''stable graph''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Beckenbach|first1=Isabel|last2=Borndörfer|first2=Ralf|date=2018-10-01|title=Hall's and Kőnig's theorem in graphs and hypergraphs|journal=Discrete Mathematics|language=en|volume=341|issue=10|pages=2753–2761|doi=10.1016/j.disc.2018.06.013|s2cid=52067804 |issn=0012-365X|doi-access=free}}</ref> Every [[bipartite graph]] is stable; this means that in every bipartite graph, the fractional matching number is an integer and it equals the integral matching number.

In an arbitrary graph,  <math>\nu(G) \geq \tfrac{2}{3} \nu^*(G).</math><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Füredi|first=Zoltán|date=1981-06-01|title=Maximum degree and fractional matchings in uniform hypergraphs|journal=Combinatorica|language=en|volume=1|issue=2|pages=155–162|doi=10.1007/BF02579271|s2cid=10530732|issn=1439-6912}}</ref> The fractional matching number is either an integer or a [[half-integer]].<ref>{{cite book|title = Fractional Graph Theory: A Rational Approach to the Theory of Graphs | last1 = Scheinerman | first1=Edward R. |last2 = Ullman | first2 = Daniel H. | year = 1997 | publisher = John Wiley & Sons | url = https://www.ams.jhu.edu/ers/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/fgt.pdf | access-date = November 13, 2025 | page = 15}}</ref>

== Matrix presentation ==
For a bipartite graph <math>G=(X,Y,E)</math>, a fractional matching can be presented as a matrix with <math>|X|</math> rows and <math>|Y|</math> columns. The value of the entry in row <math>x</math> and column <math>y</math> is the fraction of the edge <math>(x,y)</math>.

== Perfect fractional matching ==
A fractional matching is called ''perfect'' if the sum of weights adjacent to each vertex is exactly one. The size of a perfect matching is exactly <math>|V|/2</math>.

In a [[bipartite graph]] <math>G=(X,Y,E)</math>, a fractional matching is called <math>X</math>-''perfect'' if the sum of weights adjacent to each vertex of <math>X</math> is exactly one. The size of an <math>X</math>-perfect fractional matching is exactly <math>|X|</math>.

For a bipartite graph <math>G=(X,Y,E)</math>, the following are equivalent:
*<math>G</math> admits an <math>X</math>-perfect integral matching,
*<math>G</math> admits an <math>X</math>-perfect fractional matching, and
*<math>G</math> satisfies the condition to [[Hall's marriage theorem]].

The first condition implies the second because an integral matching is a fractional matching. The second implies the third because, for each subset <math>W\subset X</math>, the sum of weights incident to vertices of <math>W</math> is <math>W</math>, so the edges adjacent to them are necessarily adjacent to at least <math>W</math> vertices of <math>Y</math>.  By [[Hall's marriage theorem]], the last condition implies the first one.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Aharoni | first = Ron | author-link = Ron Aharoni
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02582958
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Graphs and Combinatorics]]
 | mr = 951021
 | pages = 303–304
 | title = Matchings in {{mvar|n}}-partite {{mvar|n}}-graphs
 | volume = 1
 | year = 1985}}</ref>

In a general graph, the above conditions are not equivalent – the largest fractional matching can be larger than the largest integral matching. For example, a 3-cycle admits a perfect fractional matching of size <math>\tfrac32</math> (the fraction of every edge is <math>\tfrac32</math>), but does not admit a perfect integral matching – its largest integral matching is of size one.

== Algorithmic aspects ==
A largest fractional matching in a graph can be found by [[linear programming]], or alternatively by a [[Maximum flow problem|maximum flow algorithm]]. In a bipartite graph, it is possible to convert a maximum fractional matching to a maximum integral matching of the same size. This leads to a polynomial-time algorithm for finding a [[Maximum cardinality matching|maximum matching]] in a bipartite graph.<ref name=":2">{{Cite Gartner Matousek 2006}}</ref>

If <math>G=(X,Y,E)</math> is a bipartite graph with <math>|X|=|Y|=n</math>, and <math>M</math> is a perfect fractional matching, then the matrix representation of <math>M</math> is a [[doubly stochastic matrix]] – the sum of elements in each row and each column is one. [[Birkhoff's algorithm]] can be used to decompose the matrix into a convex sum of at most <math>n^2-2n+2</math> [[Permutation matrix|permutation matrices]]. This corresponds to decomposing <math>M</math> into a [[convex combination]] of at most <math>n^2-2n+2</math> perfect matchings.

=== Maximum-cardinality fractional matching ===
A fractional matching of maximum cardinality (i.e., maximum sum of fractions) can be found by [[linear programming]]. There is also a [[strongly-polynomial time]] algorithm,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bourjolly|first1=Jean-Marie|last2=Pulleyblank|first2=William R.|date=1989-01-01|title=König-Egerváry graphs, 2-bicritical graphs and fractional matchings|journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics|language=en|volume=24|issue=1|pages=63–82|doi=10.1016/0166-218X(92)90273-D|issn=0166-218X|doi-access=free}}</ref> using [[augmenting path]]s, that runs in time <math>O(|V|\cdot|E|)</math>.

=== Maximum-weight fractional matching ===
Suppose each edge on the graph has a weight. A fractional matching of maximum weight in a graph can be found by [[linear programming]]. In a bipartite graph, it is possible to convert a maximum-weight fractional matching to a maximum-weight integral matching of the same size, in the following way:<ref>{{Cite web|last=Vazirani|first=Umesh|date=2012|title=Maximum Weighted Matchings|url=https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~satishr/cs270/sp11/rough-notes/matching.pdf|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=U. C. Berkeley}}</ref>

* Let <math>f</math> be the fractional matching. 
* Let <math>H</math> be a subgraph of <math>G</math> containing only the edges <math>e</math> with non-integral fraction, <math>0<f(e)<1</math>.
* If <math>H</math> is empty, then <math>f</math> already describes an integral matching.
* if <math>H</math> has a cycle, then it must be even-length (since the graph is bipartite). One can construct a new fractional matching <math>f_1</math> by transferring a small fraction <math>\varepsilon</math> from edges in even positions around the cycle to edges in odd positions, and a new fractional matching <math>f_2</math> by transferring <math>\varepsilon</math> from odd edges to even edges. Since <math>f</math> is the average of <math>f_1</math> and <math>f_2</math>, the weight of <math>f</math> is the average between the weight of <math>f_1</math> and of <math>f_2</math>. Since <math>f</math> has maximum weight, all three matchings must have the same weight. There exists a choice of <math>\varepsilon</math> for which at least one of <math>f_1</math> and <math>f_2</math> has fewer edges with non-integral fraction. Continuing in the same way leads to an integral matching of the same weight.
*Supposing that <math>H</math> has no cycle, let <math>P</math> be a longest path in <math>H</math>. As above, one can construct two matchings <math>f_1</math> and <math>f_2</math> by transferring <math>\varepsilon</math> from edges in even positions along the path to edges in odd positions, or vice versa. Because <math>P</math> is a longest path, its endpoints have no other edges of <math>H</math> incident to them, and any incident edges in <math>G\setminus H</math> must have zero as their fraction, so this transfer cannot overload these vertices. Again <math>f_1</math> and <math>f_2</math> must have maximum weight, and at least one of them has fewer non-integral fractions.

== Fractional matching polytope ==
Given a graph <math>G=(V,E)</math>, the '''fractional matching polytope''' of <math>G</math> is a [[convex polytope]] that represents all possible fractional matchings of <math>G</math>. It is a polytope in <math>\mathbb{R}^{|E|}</math> – the <math>|E|</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]. Each point <math>(x_1,\dots,x_{|E|})</math> in the polytope represents a matching in which, for some numbering of the edges as <math>e_1,\dots,e_{|E|}</math>, the fraction of each edge is <math>f(e_i)=x_i</math>. This polytope is defined by <math>|E|</math> non-negativity constraints (<math>x_i\ge 0</math> for all <math>i=1,\dots,|E|</math>) and <math>|V|</math> vertex constraints (the sum of <math>x_i</math>, for all edges <math>e_i</math> that are adjacent to a vertex <math>v</math>, is at most one).

For a bipartite graph, this is the [[matching polytope]], the [[convex hull]] of the points in <math>\mathbb{R}^{|E|}</math> that correspond to integral matchings. Thus, in this case, the vertices of the polytope are all integral. For a non-bipartite graph, the fractional matching polytope is a superset of the matching polytope.
